items.prompt: Which of these is 'state,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A cart count that changes as the user adds items
The name of the CSS file linked in the page's head
The version number of the framework the page uses
A comment left in the source code explaining a function
items.explanation: State is data that determines what the page currently shows and changes over time from user actions — a cart count is a textbook example; a CSS filename, a framework version, and a code comment don't change in response to anything the user does on the page.

items.prompt: A single text input's currently-typed value, read by nothing else on the page, is an example of what?
choices: Component state
A single source of truth shared across the app
Unidirectional data flow
A render function
items.explanation: Component state is state that belongs to one part of the UI — it should stay local as long as only that one component needs it, exactly the case here.

items.prompt: A dropdown menu's 'open or closed' flag is read only by the dropdown itself. Should it be lifted to a shared store?
choices: No — nothing else needs it, so it should stay local component state
Yes — all boolean flags must always live in a global store
Yes — because any state must eventually be shared
No — booleans specifically can never be treated as state
items.explanation: The rule is to keep state in the smallest place that serves everyone who needs it. If only the dropdown reads and changes the flag, it should stay local — lifting it would add coordination overhead for no benefit.

items.prompt: Is a value that's set once when the page loads and never changes afterward best described as 'state'?
choices: No — state specifically refers to data that can change over time in response to actions
Yes — anything stored in a variable counts as state
Yes, but only if it's stored in an object instead of a primitive
No — only values fetched from a server can be state
items.explanation: The defining feature of state is that it changes over time as the user interacts with the page. A value fixed at load time and never updated again doesn't have that property, so calling it 'state' doesn't add anything useful.

items.prompt: Two sibling components both need to read and react to the same toggle value. Should that toggle stay as component state inside just one of them?
choices: No — once more than one part of the UI needs to read or change it, it should move outward to a common owner
Yes — component state should never move, no matter how many components need it
Yes, as long as the two components are visually next to each other on the page
No — it should be deleted and replaced with a prop drilled from nowhere
items.explanation: Component state is meant to stay local only 'while only that component needs it.' Once a second component needs to read or change the same value, it should be lifted to a shared owner rather than duplicated.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a kind of data to whether it's 'state' in this unit's sense?
choices: Whether a menu is open (state) vs. the literal text of a button's label defined in the source code (not state)
The user's current scroll position (not state) vs. a hardcoded page title (state)
Both are state, since anything rendered on the page counts
Neither is state, since state only describes server-side data
items.explanation: A menu's open/closed flag changes over time from user actions — that's state. A button label hardcoded in the source never changes at runtime, so it isn't state, even though it's rendered on the page.

items.prompt: What's the difference between 'state' in general and 'component state' specifically?
choices: Component state is state that belongs to one part of the UI; state in general is the broader category that includes values shared more widely too
Component state is a value that never changes, while state in general always changes
There's no difference at all — the two terms are strict synonyms with no distinction
Component state only exists in server-rendered pages, never in the browser
items.explanation: 'State' is the general term for data that drives what's shown and changes over time. 'Component state' narrows that to state scoped to one UI part — it's a specific case, not a separate kind of thing.

items.prompt: A 'draft comment' textarea's current text is read by the comment box itself and nothing else yet. Where should it live right now?
choices: As local component state in the comment box
In a focused store shared by distant parts of the page
In one giant global object alongside every other value on the page
It shouldn't be tracked as state at all
items.explanation: With only one component reading and changing it, the draft text belongs as local component state — moving it further out before anything else needs it would add unnecessary coordination for no benefit.

items.prompt: What is 'state,' as this unit defines it?
choices: The data that determines what a page currently shows, which can change over time in response to user actions
The CSS styles and class names applied to an already-rendered element
The initial HTML markup a server sends before any JavaScript starts running
A permanent record of every action a user has ever taken on the page
items.explanation: State is specifically the data driving what's currently displayed — a cart count, a form value, whether a menu is open — and it changes as the user interacts with the page.
items.reference:
State
🔢 Drives what the page shows
🔁 Changes over time from actions
Why: state is the thing that can drift out of sync when it's copied in multiple places.
items.reflection: The word 'state' shows up far outside UI code too: a database transaction, a game character, a traffic light, even a conversation ('where did we leave things?') all have state that changes over time and drives what happens next. Where have you seen the same word used for something that isn't a webpage at all?

items.prompt: A 'logged in as' label appears in both the header and a settings page, both reading the same underlying user object. Is that user object itself 'component state'?
choices: No — once more than one, unrelated part of the UI needs to read it, it's no longer scoped to a single component; it needs a shared owner, even though each display is still just rendering it
Yes — anything displayed inside a component is automatically that component's state
No — because user data fetched from a server is never state
Yes, as long as the header and settings page are both written by the same developer
items.explanation: Component state means state scoped to one part of the UI. The moment two unrelated displays need the same value, it has outgrown 'component state' and needs a shared owner — the header and settings page are exactly that case.

items.prompt: A junior developer argues: 'this input's typed-but-not-yet-submitted text is state, so it belongs in the app's single global store, same as the cart count.' What's wrong with that reasoning?
choices: It conflates 'this is state' with 'this belongs in the global store' — state should live in the smallest place that serves everyone who needs it, and an input only read by itself should stay local
Nothing is wrong — every piece of state must live in exactly one global store, no exceptions
The typed text isn't actually state at all, so the question is moot
Global stores can only ever hold numeric values like counts, never text
items.explanation: Being 'state' doesn't imply a specific location. The rule is to scope state to the smallest owner that still serves every reader — an input nobody else reads should stay local component state, not get pulled into a shared store just because it technically qualifies as state.

items.prompt: A sidebar widget silently keeps its own local copy of the cart count, separate from the header and drawer badges, instead of reading the shared value. What category of problem does this risk, even if the widget's copy starts out correct?
choices: It reintroduces the exact single-source-of-truth problem this unit is about — a separate copy of the same state that can silently drift out of sync with the others
No problem at all, since the widget's copy began with the correct number
A security vulnerability, since cart counts are sensitive data
A performance problem only, with no risk of incorrect values
items.explanation: The danger isn't the copy's starting value — it's that a separate copy has no mechanism forcing it to stay in sync with later changes, which is precisely the two-badge bug's shape, just with a third display this time.

items.prompt: What does 'single source of truth' mean?
choices: Keeping exactly one authoritative copy of a piece of state, so every display reads from the same place
Storing all of a page's data together inside a single file on the server
Only allowing one developer to edit any of the state-related code
Using a single shared CSS class to style every stateful element
items.explanation: A single source of truth means one authoritative value per piece of state — not one giant shared variable for everything, just no separate driftable copies of the same value.

items.prompt: If a header badge and a drawer badge each keep their own separate count variable, do they have a single source of truth?
choices: No — each badge has its own copy, so there's no single authoritative value either reads from
Yes, as long as both variables start out equal to each other
Yes, because they're both just numbers showing the same concept
It depends only on which badge was written first
items.explanation: Two separate variables tracking 'the same' value is exactly the absence of a single source of truth — there's no one place that's authoritative, so the two copies can disagree.

items.prompt: Does 'single source of truth' mean putting every unrelated value on the page into one shared object?
choices: No — it means one authoritative copy per piece of state, not collapsing all state into one object
Yes — a single source of truth requires exactly one object for the whole page
Yes, but only for pages with fewer than five stateful values
No, because single source of truth doesn't apply to objects, only primitives
items.explanation: The idea applies per piece of state. Cart count, theme, and a draft comment can each have their own single source of truth without being merged into one giant shared object.

items.prompt: A theme toggle's 'dark mode on/off' value is read directly from one shared variable by every component that needs it. Does this have a single source of truth?
choices: Yes — every reader reads from the same authoritative value, with no separate copies
No — a single source of truth requires at least two components to disagree
No, because theme values are never eligible to be a single source of truth
It depends on how many components read the variable
items.explanation: Having one authoritative value that every display reads from is exactly what a single source of truth is — the number of readers doesn't change that, as long as none of them keep a separate copy.

items.prompt: Why can two displays disagree even though the underlying count variable itself is always correct?
choices: Because a display can be updated inconsistently, independent of whether the one shared value is correct
They can never disagree if the underlying variable is correct
Because JavaScript numbers are inherently imprecise
Because displays always read a stale cached copy from the server
items.explanation: A single source of truth being correct doesn't guarantee every display reflects it — if a display isn't reliably updated whenever that value changes, it can still show something stale even though the authoritative value itself is fine.

items.prompt: A notification count appears in a tab title and in a bell icon, both reading the same shared counter. One day a developer adds code that lets the bell icon increment its own local copy directly. What happens to the single source of truth?
choices: It's broken — the bell icon now has a second, separate copy that can drift from the shared counter
Nothing changes, since both values started out equal
The single source of truth is strengthened, since now two values confirm each other
This has no effect on single source of truth, only on performance
items.explanation: The moment the bell icon keeps and updates its own copy instead of reading the shared counter, there are now two authoritative-looking values — exactly the condition that lets displays disagree.

items.prompt: Which setup has a single source of truth for 'is the shopping cart empty'?
choices: A boolean computed on demand from the cart's one shared item list, wherever it's needed
A separate boolean cached by each of three different components, set once and never refreshed
Both setups equally have a single source of truth
Neither setup can have a single source of truth, since it's a derived value
items.explanation: Deriving the boolean fresh from the one shared list every time keeps a single authoritative source. Three separately cached booleans are three copies that can each go stale independently.

items.prompt: Is having a single source of truth the same thing as having unidirectional data flow?
choices: No — single source of truth is about where state lives (one authoritative copy); unidirectional data flow is about how changes reach every display
Yes, the two terms describe the exact same mechanism
No, because single source of truth only applies to numbers
Yes, but only when the state is stored in a database
items.explanation: They're related but distinct: single source of truth is about not having duplicate copies of a value, while unidirectional data flow is about the path a change takes to reach every display of that value.

items.prompt: In the naive cart example, why don't the header and drawer badges share a single source of truth?
choices: Each badge is updated directly by whichever handler happens to touch it, rather than both reading from one shared value
They do already share a single source of truth, which is why the bug is surprising
The badges live in separate files, and separate files inherently prevent sharing state
JavaScript itself doesn't allow two DOM elements to reflect the same variable
items.explanation: In the naive version, `count` exists, but the badges aren't derived from it consistently — each handler decides on its own which badges to touch, so there's no enforced single source of truth in practice.
items.reference:
Single source of truth
1️⃣ One authoritative value
👀 Every display reads from it
Why: separate copies of the same value are what let displays disagree.
items.reflection: Single source of truth isn't a web-only idea: a company with three spreadsheets each claiming to be 'the' headcount number, or two clocks in a house showing different times, both fail the same way a two-badge bug does. Where have you seen the same value tracked in more than one place quietly go out of sync?

items.prompt: A team 'fixes' a drifting single source of truth bug by adding a background job that periodically re-syncs every display's cached copy back to the real count every 5 seconds. Does this restore a true single source of truth?
choices: No — it papers over the symptom; the displays still hold independent copies that can be wrong for up to 5 seconds, instead of always reading the one authoritative value directly
Yes — periodic re-sync is functionally identical to having one authoritative value
Yes, as long as the sync interval is under 10 seconds
No, because background jobs can never read application state
items.explanation: A single source of truth means every display reads the authoritative value directly (or is notified immediately when it changes) — not that drifted copies get periodically patched. The periodic re-sync is a workaround for the symptom, not a fix for the missing single source of truth.

items.prompt: A form's validity is computed independently by both the submit button's disabled logic and the field's red-border logic, each re-deriving it from the field values using separately written validation code. Even if both pieces of logic are currently identical, what risk does this setup carry that a single shared validity check wouldn't?
choices: A future edit to one copy of the validation logic (say, adding a new rule) can be missed in the other, making the border and button disagree about validity
No risk at all, since both pieces of logic read the same field values
The risk only exists if the field values themselves are stored on a server
This setup is strictly better, since duplicated logic runs faster
items.explanation: Two independently written copies of 'is this valid' logic are two sources of truth in disguise — they happen to agree today, but nothing forces them to stay in sync when one is edited and the other isn't, which is exactly the two-badge bug's shape applied to validation.

items.prompt: A developer argues that caching a computed value (like a cart's total price) in a variable, instead of recomputing it from the item list every time, automatically breaks single source of truth. Is that necessarily true?
choices: Not necessarily — it's only broken if the cache can go stale (nothing updates it when the item list changes); a cache that's always correctly recomputed whenever its inputs change still has one true source, the item list, with the cached value just reflecting it reliably
Yes — any cached or derived value always breaks single source of truth by definition
No — caching a value always preserves single source of truth automatically with no extra work
It depends only on whether the value is a number or an object
items.explanation: The item list remains the one real source of truth; a cached total is fine as long as it's reliably recomputed whenever the list changes (the same unidirectional discipline this unit covers) — the risk is a cache that's forgotten and goes stale, not caching itself.

items.prompt: What is 'unidirectional data flow'?
choices: A discipline where state only changes through one defined path: an action updates state, then the update triggers re-rendering everything that depends on it
A rule saying that page data can only be read one single time per page load
A network protocol that sends data in only one direction between client and server
A CSS layout technique for arranging elements into a single vertical column
items.explanation: Unidirectional data flow is specifically about the path a change takes: action → state update → render — not about network direction or layout.

items.prompt: What is a 'render function,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Code that takes the current state and produces what the page should show, run every time the state changes
A function that generates random placeholder values purely for testing
A function that only ever runs once, the very first time the page loads
A function whose only job is sending data off to a server
items.explanation: A render function's job is to reflect state onto the page consistently — it's called whenever state changes, rather than being invoked inconsistently by individual handlers.

items.prompt: In unidirectional data flow, what comes right after 'an action updates state'?
choices: The update triggers re-rendering everything that depends on that state
The action directly edits one specific display element
The browser reloads the entire page from the server
Nothing — the loop ends there until the next page load
items.explanation: The defined path is action → state update → render. Skipping straight from an action to one display, or stopping after the state update, isn't the loop this unit describes.

items.prompt: If a button's click handler directly sets a specific badge's text, bypassing any shared state update, is that handler acting as a render function?
choices: No — a render function reflects the current state consistently; a handler that pokes one display directly is exactly the scattered-update pattern this unit moves away from
Yes — any code that changes what's displayed counts as a render function
Yes, as long as the handler runs on every click
No, because render functions can only run on page load
items.explanation: A render function is defined by reflecting state consistently, triggered by state changes — a handler that reaches in and edits one display directly, without going through state, is the opposite pattern.

items.prompt: Why is a render function supposed to run 'every time the state changes' rather than being called by hand from inside specific handlers?
choices: So every display stays consistent automatically, instead of depending on each handler remembering to call it
Because render functions are too slow to call more than once
Because handlers aren't technically allowed to call functions
It doesn't matter when it runs, as long as it eventually runs once
items.explanation: Tying the render function to every state change (rather than to specific handlers remembering to call it) is what removes the risk of a handler forgetting — the exact failure mode from the two-badge bug.

items.prompt: Is 'unidirectional' in 'unidirectional data flow' describing network traffic direction (client to server)?
choices: No — it describes the one-way path a state change takes through a page: action, then state update, then render
Yes, it specifically means requests only ever go from client to server, never the reverse
Yes, it means a server can never send a response back to a client
No, it describes which way text reads on the page, left-to-right vs. right-to-left
items.explanation: The term is about the direction a UI update flows (action → state → render), not about network request direction or text direction — those are unrelated meanings of similar-sounding words.

items.prompt: A render function reads the current state and updates a badge's text. Does the render function also decide when the count should increase?
choices: No — deciding when state changes is the action's job; the render function only reflects whatever the state already is
Yes — render functions are responsible for deciding what the next state should be
Yes, but only for numeric state like counts
It depends on which framework is being used
items.explanation: In the action → state update → render loop, the action decides what changes; the render function's only job is to reflect the resulting state — mixing those roles is exactly the 'logic inside render' failure mode this unit warns about.

items.prompt: Two different render functions, one for the header badge and one for the drawer badge, both run every time the shared count state changes. Is this consistent with unidirectional data flow?
choices: Yes — unidirectional data flow allows any number of render functions, as long as all of them are triggered by the same state change rather than by individual handlers
No — unidirectional data flow requires exactly one render function per page
No — having more than one display means the flow is no longer unidirectional
Yes, but only if both render functions are defined in the same file
items.explanation: Unidirectional data flow doesn't limit how many displays or render functions exist — it only requires that every one of them be reached through the same action → state update → render path, which both badges are here.

items.prompt: In the naive cart example, which part of unidirectional data flow is missing?
choices: There's no consistent 'state update triggers render for every display' step — displays are updated individually inside each action
There's no action at all involved — the badges somehow update themselves automatically
There's no state at all in the naive version — the badges are simply hardcoded numbers
There's no render step at all, since the DOM is never actually touched
items.explanation: The naive version has actions (button clicks) and eventually reaches state (the count), but skips the consistent render step — each handler decides individually which displays to touch instead of every display reacting to the same state change.
items.reference:
Unidirectional data flow
🖱️ Action
➡️ State update
➡️ Render (every display)
Why: no shortcut exists from an action straight to one specific display.
items.reflection: The action → state → render loop echoes a pattern used far outside UI code: an event sourcing system (event → new state → projections), or even a thermostat (temperature reading → target comparison → heater on/off) — a trigger, a state update, then every consumer reacting the same way. Where else have you seen a system insist changes flow through one funnel instead of many shortcuts?

items.prompt: In L3's fixed version, what plays the role of the render function for the header badge?
choices: The subscriber callback that sets `headerBadge.textContent` whenever the store notifies it
The `addItem` function, which updates the badge as a side effect
The `createCartStore` function itself, each time it's called
The `getState` function, every time its return value is read
items.explanation: The subscriber callback is what takes the current state and updates the header badge — it runs every time the store's state changes, which is exactly the render function's job.
items.reference:
Render function
📥 Takes current state
📤 Produces what the page shows
Why: a render function run consistently is what replaces scattered, handler-specific updates.

items.prompt: A developer writes a render function that, while updating the badge's text, also decides to send an analytics event only when the count crosses 10. Is putting that decision inside the render function consistent with unidirectional data flow?
choices: No — deciding 'when' something should happen is logic that belongs in the action, not scattered into a render function whose only job should be reflecting state
Yes — render functions are free to contain any logic, including deciding when side effects fire
Yes, as long as the analytics event doesn't change any state itself
No, because render functions are not allowed to run any code besides DOM updates
items.explanation: This is the 'logic inside render' failure mode — a render function should be a pure reflection of state; decisions about when something should happen belong in the action that changes the state, kept separate from the function that just displays it.

items.prompt: A new requirement arrives: whenever the cart count changes, also update the page's document title to include it. Following unidirectional data flow strictly, what's the correct way to add this?
choices: Add another render function (or subscriber) that also reacts to the same state change — not a new direct call inserted into the existing action handlers
Add a line inside `addItem` and every other action that changes the count, setting `document.title` directly from each one
This can't be done without abandoning unidirectional data flow entirely
Only one render function is allowed to exist per state value, so this requirement can't be met
items.explanation: The point of the loop is that any number of displays — including a brand-new one like the document title — can react to the same state change by registering their own render step, without editing the actions that caused the change. Reaching into every action handler to add the title update would recreate the exact scattered-update risk this unit is about.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, which two places display the cart count?
choices: A header badge and a cart drawer badge
A header badge and the browser tab title
A product page and a checkout page
A header badge and an email receipt
items.explanation: The scenario is specifically about a header badge and a cart drawer badge, both meant to show the same cart item count.

items.prompt: After the shopper adds one item from the product page, what do both badges show?
choices: They show different numbers even after the first action
items.explanation: The first action (adding from the product page) correctly updates both badges to 1 — the bug only appears after the second action, from quick buy.

items.prompt: After the shopper then uses the quick-buy shortcut, what does the drawer badge show?
choices: A blank value
items.explanation: Quick buy correctly updates the drawer badge to 2 — it's the header badge, not the drawer badge, that's left behind.

items.prompt: After quick buy, what does the header badge show?
choices: 1 — it's stuck at the value from before quick buy ran
2 — it updates correctly along with the drawer
0 — it resets
An error message
items.explanation: The header badge is left at 1 because the quick-buy handler was never written to update it — the exact mismatch the scenario describes.

items.prompt: Is the two-badge bug caused by the cart count being calculated wrong?
choices: No — the count itself is correct the whole time
Yes — the count increments by the wrong amount
Yes — the count resets unexpectedly
There's no way to know without seeing the server logs
items.explanation: The count is accurate after both actions — the bug is entirely about which displays get updated, not about the arithmetic.

items.prompt: What's actually missing from the quick-buy button's click handler?
choices: A line that updates the header badge
Any code that updates the cart count at all
A network request to the server
A CSS class on the button itself
items.explanation: The quick-buy handler correctly updates the count and the drawer badge — it's simply never told to also touch the header badge.

items.prompt: If a third action (say, 'remove from cart') is added later and also forgets to update the header badge, is that a coincidence?
choices: No — it's the same structural risk repeating: any new handler can independently forget a display unless something forces it not to
Yes, entirely unrelated to the original bug
No, but only because the same developer wrote both handlers
It can't happen again once the first bug is reported
items.explanation: The scenario's point is structural: nothing prevents a future handler from repeating exactly the same mistake, since each handler independently decides which displays to touch.

items.prompt: Before the quick-buy action runs, were the header and drawer badges ever out of sync?
choices: No — they agreed (both showed 1) right after the first action, and only diverged after the second
Yes, they disagreed from the very first action
Yes, but only because of a network delay
There's no information about their state before quick buy
items.explanation: The scenario is specific: both badges agree after the first action, and the divergence only appears once the second handler (quick buy) runs.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, why does the header badge end up wrong after the quick-buy action, even though the underlying count is correct?
choices: The quick-buy handler updates the drawer badge but was never written to also update the header badge
The count variable itself silently becomes incorrect after the quick-buy action runs
The header badge is a read-only element that can never be updated by any code
The product-page handler runs after the quick-buy handler and overwrites its result
items.explanation: The count is accurate; the header badge is simply never told to update inside the quick-buy handler — a missing line in one specific handler, not a data problem.
items.reference:
Why they diverge
✅ count is correct
🚫 header badge update is missing
Why: the number is right; the display update was simply never wired up for this action.
items.reflection: This exact shape — the underlying number is right, but one of its displays silently stops reflecting it — shows up anywhere a value is shown more than once: a bank balance shown in an app and a receipt printed earlier, or two clocks in different rooms that used to agree. Where have you seen two displays of 'the same fact' quietly go out of sync even though the real fact never changed?

items.prompt: A third entry point, 'add via voice assistant,' is added later and correctly increments the count and updates both existing badges — because its author happened to copy the product-page handler's code. Has the underlying structural risk from the two-badge bug been fixed?
choices: No — this specific handler happened to get it right, but any future handler can still independently forget a display; nothing in the structure prevents the next copy-paste from missing one
Yes — once every current handler updates every current display, the bug class is gone for good
Yes, because copying an existing handler's code guarantees correctness forever
No, because adding any new entry point always reintroduces the bug immediately
items.explanation: Getting the current set of handlers right by careful copying doesn't remove the underlying risk — it's still possible (even likely, over enough handlers) for a future one to miss a display, because nothing in the code's structure forces every handler to touch every display.

items.prompt: Suppose instead of adding an item, the bug were about *removing* one: the drawer badge decrements correctly but the header badge doesn't. Is this still the same underlying problem as the original two-badge bug?
choices: Yes — it's the identical structural shape (a handler updates one display but not another); only the specific action (remove instead of add) changed
No — removing is a fundamentally different kind of bug that needs a different kind of fix
Yes, but only if the count is also wrong, which it isn't said to be
No, because decrementing can never cause a display mismatch
items.explanation: The scenario is defined by its shape, not its specific action — any handler (add, remove, or anything else) that updates some displays but not others while the underlying value stays correct reproduces the exact same bug.

items.prompt: If the header badge had been missing from the page's HTML entirely (never existing as an element at all), would that be the same bug as the one in this scenario?
choices: No — a missing element is a different failure (nothing to update at all); this scenario's bug is that a real, existing display simply isn't told about a specific action
Yes — any time the header shows the wrong thing, it's the identical bug regardless of cause
No, because a missing element can never cause a visible mismatch
Yes, since both cases involve the word 'header badge'
items.explanation: The scenario specifically involves a header badge that exists and is correctly updated by one handler but not another — a missing element altogether would be a different problem (nothing to even target), not the same structural gap this unit is diagnosing.

items.prompt: In L2's unidirectional loop diagram, what happens immediately after an action fires?
choices: The state update step runs
Every display updates itself directly, independent of state
The action fires again, in a loop
Nothing — actions and state are unrelated in the diagram
items.explanation: The loop's first step after an action is always the state update — actions never touch a display directly in this model.

items.prompt: In the diagram, what happens right after the state update step?
choices: Render runs, and every subscriber re-reads the state
The action that triggered it runs a second time
The page reloads from the server
Nothing further happens until the user clicks again
items.explanation: Render is the step right after state update — it's what reaches every display, rather than the state update reaching displays directly.

items.prompt: Is there any arrow in the diagram that goes directly from 'action' to a specific display, like the header badge?
choices: No — every path from an action to a display passes through state update and render first
Yes — each display has its own direct arrow from the actions that affect it
Yes, but only the header badge gets a direct arrow like that
The diagram doesn't actually include any displays as nodes at all
items.explanation: The absence of a direct action-to-display arrow is the whole point of the diagram — it's exactly the shortcut that caused the header badge to be skipped in the naive version.

items.prompt: In the diagram, how many displays can read from the render step?
choices: Any number — both the header badge and drawer badge read from the same render step
Exactly one — only a single display is allowed per loop
